opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, and honestly one we debate a lot internally. There's a real temptation in the field right now to say, "Let's just build a world model that predicts the future in full sensor fidelity: every pixel of camera, every lidar point." It's appealing because it's self-supervised. You have essentially unlimited data, and you don't need humans to label anything.

But I think you have to ask what that detail actually buys you for driving. A lot of what's in a raw sensor stream is irrelevant to the decision you need to make. Exactly how the leaves on a tree move, or the texture of a building facade, doesn't matter much. If you force a model to spend its capacity reconstructing all of that, you may be optimizing for the wrong thing. The model can get very good at rendering plausible-looking futures while still being mediocre at the things that matter: will that pedestrian step off the curb, is that car going to cut in, where's the drivable space.

So the way I tend to think about it is a spectrum. At one end you have very compact, structured representations: objects, tracks, maps, behavior predictions. These are efficient, interpretable, and directly useful for planning, but they're lossy. You can miss things your ontology didn't anticipate, like an unusual object or a subtle cue like someone waving you through. At the other end you have full sensor prediction, which captures everything but is expensive and not targeted.

The sweet spot, in my view, is somewhere in between. Rich sensor-level prediction is very valuable as a learning signal and for simulation. If you want to test a driving policy closed-loop, you need a simulator that can produce realistic sensor inputs when the car does something different from what happened in the logs. There, fidelity really matters, because your onboard stack consumes those sensors. Generative sensor models are also great pretraining objectives; they help the model learn general structure about the world.

But for the onboard driving model itself, I'd rather predict the future in a learned, more abstract space that's shaped by what matters for the task, possibly with some auxiliary sensor reconstruction to keep it grounded. And you want to weigh errors by their consequences. A small mistake about a pedestrian's intent is much worse than getting the sky color wrong.

So in short: rich sensor prediction is extremely valuable for simulation, evaluation, and representation learning, but it's not automatically what you want your driver to be optimizing. The key is aligning what the model spends its capacity on with what makes driving safe.

r001.rationale: The response says much raw sensor detail is irrelevant to driving decisions and that modeling it can spend capacity on the wrong things, while task-relevant behavior and drivable space matter more.

r002.rationale: It describes rich sensor prediction as valuable for realistic closed-loop simulation, while saying the onboard driving model should optimize a more task-shaped representation and that sensor prediction is not automatically what the driver should optimize.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question we've thought about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it depends on what you're trying to get out of the model.

If you take the pure world-model view, where you say, "I'm going to predict the next lidar sweep or the next camera frame at full fidelity," you're spending an enormous amount of capacity on things that don't matter for driving. The exact texture of the leaves on a tree, the precise reflectivity pattern on a building facade, the pattern of raindrops on the lens — none of that changes what the vehicle should do. So from a decision-making standpoint, a lot of that detail is wasted effort, and worse, it can distract the model, because the loss is dominated by pixels or points that are irrelevant.

On the other hand, I don't think you can fully dismiss it either. There's a reason generative modeling has worked so well in language and vision. When you force a model to predict the raw observations, you get a very dense, very rich training signal. You don't have to decide in advance what the important concepts are. The model discovers them because it has to in order to explain the data. And in driving, the long tail is exactly the stuff you didn't think to label. If you only supervise on boxes and tracks and lane lines, you've already baked in your assumptions about what matters.

So the way I'd frame it is: the value of predicting sensor detail is as a representation learning objective, not as an end goal. You want enough reconstruction pressure that the model learns geometry, learns dynamics, learns how agents interact and how occlusion works, but then you want to abstract away from the raw detail as quickly as possible when it comes to the parts of the system that make decisions. Predicting in some latent or semantic space, or at coarser resolution, or conditioned on what's relevant to the ego vehicle, tends to be the sweet spot.

And there's a practical angle too. Rich sensor prediction is extremely useful for simulation. If you want to close the loop and test a planner against realistic counterfactuals, being able to render what the sensors would see in a scenario that never happened is really powerful. So the same capability that looks wasteful for online driving becomes very valuable offline for evaluation and for generating training data.

So I'd say: weigh it by what it buys you in terms of learned structure and simulation fidelity, not by how pretty the reconstructions look. Pretty reconstructions are a side effect. The question is always whether the model understands the scene well enough to make the right decision.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-grained sensor details can be irrelevant to driving, but does not state that broadening prediction beyond people’s near-term behavior makes predictions less relevant.

r002.rationale: It says rich sensor prediction is useful for simulation and counterfactual evaluation, while often wasteful for online driving.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much of that detail matters for driving. There’s a lot of information in sensor data, and predicting it well could help you learn useful representations of the world. But you can also spend a lot of capacity predicting things that don’t really affect what the vehicle should do.

For example, the exact appearance of a surface may be less important than whether a pedestrian is about to enter the road. So I would judge the value of richer prediction by whether it helps us understand motion, anticipate interactions, and make better decisions, especially in situations where there’s uncertainty. Rich sensor prediction can be a useful learning objective, but ultimately we need to connect it to driving performance.

r001.rationale: The response says some sensor details may not affect driving and contrasts surface appearance with pedestrian behavior, but it does not clearly state that broadening prediction beyond people’s near-term behavior tends to make predicted content less relevant.

r002.rationale: The response discusses rich sensor prediction as a learning objective but does not mention a simulator or say that modeling sensor detail can benefit a simulator without improving autonomous driving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the question is, what detail actually matters for driving? There’s a tremendous amount of information in the sensor data, and predicting all of it is a very challenging task. But a lot of that information may not affect the decision you need to make. You need to understand where the other agents are, how they might move, and what parts of the environment are relevant to your trajectory.

That said, predicting richer sensor detail can be a useful way to learn representations, because it gives you a lot of supervision without requiring someone to label everything. So I see value in it, but I would ultimately judge it by whether it helps the system make better driving decisions. The richness of the prediction by itself isn’t the goal.
